en: Parivāra 13.
Codanākaṇḍa 1.
Anuvijjakaanuyoga (The Investigation of the Enquirer)
The investigator should ask the accuser:

"Friend, regarding this monk whom you are accusing, on what grounds do you accuse him? Do you accuse him of failure in virtue, or do you accuse him of failure in conduct, or do you accuse him of failure in view?
If he should speak thus:
“If you say, ‘I am reproving you for a failure in virtue, or I am reproving you for a failure in conduct, or I am reproving you for a failure in view,’ he should be asked:
‘But does the venerable one know what a failure in virtue is, does he know what a failure in conduct is, and does he know what a failure in view is?
If he should say this:”
“If one says, ‘Friend, I know failure in virtue; I know failure in conduct; I know failure in view,’ he should be addressed thus:
‘But what, friend, is failure in virtue?
What is failure in conduct?’”
“What is failure in view?
If he should say this:
“The four offenses involving defeat and the thirteen offenses entailing suspension—this is failure in virtue.”
“Thullaccaya, pācittiya, pāṭidesanīya, dukkaṭa, dubbhāsita—this is failure in conduct.
Wrong view, extremist view—this is failure in view. To him it should be said:
“Friend, when you accuse this bhikkhu, do you accuse him on account of what has been seen, or do you accuse him on account of what has been heard, or do you accuse him on account of suspicion?”
If he should say, "I accuse him on account of what has been seen, or I accuse him on account of what has been heard, or I accuse him on account of suspicion," he should be addressed thus:
"Friend, as for this bhikkhu whom you accuse on account of what has been seen, what have you seen? How was it seen by you?"

When was it seen by you? Where was it seen by you? Was he seen committing an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika)? Was he seen committing an offense entailing suspension from the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa)?
[Was he seen committing] a serious offense (thullaccaya) … an offense entailing confession (pācittiya) …?

“While you were seen committing an offense entailing confession, an offense of wrong-doing, or an offense of improper speech, where were you, where was this monk, what were you doing, and what was this monk doing?”
If he should say this: “Friend, I do not accuse this bhikkhu on account of what was seen; rather, I accuse him on account of what was heard,” he should be addressed thus:

“Friend, as for what you accuse this bhikkhu of on account of what was heard, what have you heard? How have you heard it? When did you hear it? Where did you hear it? Did you hear that he has committed a *pārājika* offense? … [or] a *saṅghādisesa* offense? …
a grave offense (thullaccaya) … an offense entailing confession (pācittiya) … an offense entailing acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya) …
"I have heard that he has committed an offense of wrong-doing... or an offense of improper speech;

it was heard by a bhikkhu, heard by a bhikkhunī, heard by a female trainee, heard by a male novice, heard by a female novice, heard by a male lay follower, heard by a female lay follower, or heard by kings."
“Have you heard it from the king’s ministers, have you heard it from the sectarians, or have you heard it from the disciples of the sectarians?
If he should say, “Friends, I do not reproach this bhikkhu on account of what I have heard; rather, I reproach him on account of suspicion,” then he should be told this:
“Friend, regarding this monk whom you have charged out of suspicion: what do you suspect? How do you suspect?
When did you suspect? Where did you suspect? Do you suspect that he has committed a *pārājika* offense?
Do you suspect that he has committed a *saṅghādisesa* offense? A *thullaccaya* offense?”...
an offense entailing confession (pācittiya) … an offense entailing acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya) … an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) …
"You suspect that he has committed an offense of wrong speech: you suspect it after hearing from a bhikkhu; you suspect it after hearing from a bhikkhunī;
you suspect it after hearing from a female trainee (sikkhamānā); you suspect it after hearing from a male novice (sāmaṇera); you suspect it after hearing from a female novice (sāmaṇerī);
you suspect it after hearing from a male lay follower (upāsaka); you suspect it after hearing from a female lay follower (upāsikā); [or] from kings..."
“Do you suspect it after hearing [the words] of householders, do you suspect it after hearing the words of royal ministers, do you suspect it after hearing the words of members of other sects,
or do you suspect it after hearing the words of the disciples of other sects?
“What has been seen accords with what has been seen.”
The seen merges with the seen;
depending on the seen, one does not proceed,
suspecting it to be impure.
Thus, by the person's own admission,
that Uposatha should be performed;
what has been heard accords with what was heard.
What is heard accords with what is heard;
yet one does not rely on what is heard when it is suspected of being impure.
Therefore, by the person’s own admission,
that Uposatha should be performed;
what has been perceived accords with what has been perceived.
The sensed merges with the sensed;
dependent on the sensed, one does not go beyond it,
being suspected of impurity.
Therefore, that person should perform the Uposatha by means of his admission.
What is the beginning of the formal charge (codanā), what is its middle, and what is its conclusion?

In regard to formal accusation (*codanā*), the opening procedure (*okāsakamma*) is the beginning, the performance of the act (*kiriyā*) is the middle, and the settlement (*samatha*) is the conclusion.
How many roots, how many grounds, how many planes, and in how many ways does one accuse?
There are two roots for formal accusation, three grounds, five planes, and one accuses in two ways.
What are the two roots of accusation?
Whether with foundation or without foundation—
these are the two roots of accusation.
What are the three grounds for an accusation?
By what has been seen, by what has been heard, and by suspicion—
these are the three grounds for an accusation.
What are the five grounds for admonition?

One will speak at the proper time, not at an improper time; one will speak what is true, not what is untrue; one will speak gently, not harshly; one will speak in a way that is beneficial, not in a way that is unbeneficial; one will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hatred.
These are the five grounds for admonition.
In what two ways does he reprove?
He reproves either by body or by speech—
it is in these two ways that he reproves.
2. The Procedure for the Accuser and Others.
How should one proceed as an accuser?
How should one proceed as the accused?
How should the Saṅgha proceed?
How should the investigator proceed?
How should the accuser proceed?
One who reproves should reprove another after establishing oneself in five qualities:

"I will speak at the proper time, not at an improper time; I will speak what is true, not what is untrue; I will speak gently, not harshly; I will speak in a way that is beneficial, not in a way that is unbeneficial; I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hatred.
This is how one who reproves should proceed.
"How should one who has been accused conduct himself?
"One who has been accused should conduct himself according to two qualities:
truthfulness and composure."
One who has been censured should act in this way.
How should the Saṅgha act?
The Saṅgha should know whether [the matter] has been properly investigated or not.
The Saṅgha should proceed in this manner.
How should the investigator proceed?

The investigator should resolve that legal issue in accordance with the Dhamma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Teacher’s instruction—by whatever means that legal issue is settled, in that same way it should be resolved.
The investigator should proceed in this way:
"For what purpose is the Uposatha?
For what reason is the Pavāraṇā?"
For what purpose is probation (parivāsa)?
For what reason is sending back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanā)?
For what purpose is the trial period (mānatta)?
For what purpose is the act of restoration?
The Uposatha is for the sake of concord;
the Pavāraṇā is for the sake of purification.
Parivāsa is for the purpose of mānatta;
mūlāyapaṭikassanā is for the purpose of restraint;
mānatta is for the purpose of rehabilitation.
The rehabilitation is for the sake of purification.
If one reviles elders out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion, [one must undergo the abbhāna penance].
With the breakup of the body, the one of poor wisdom,
whose faculties are worn away and impaired,
goes to hell, being dull-witted.
Nor is there reverence for the training;
nor does one rely on material gain,
nor does one rely on a person.
Avoiding both of these, act according to the Dhamma.
3. The Accuser’s Self-Scorching.
One who is angry and resentful,
fierce and abusive,
who charges another with an offense when there is no offense—
Such an accuser burns himself up.
He whispers into the ear, he looks askance, he acts with pretense,
follows a wrong path, and pursues evil ways.
One who imputes an offense where there is no offense burns himself; such an accuser destroys his own self.
He accuses at an improper time and with what is untrue.
With harsh words that are unbeneficial,
one who harbors hatred within reproaches another, not with a mind of loving-kindness;
he imputes an offense where there is no offense.
Such a reprover burns himself;
he does not know what is Dhamma and what is non-Dhamma,
being unskilled in the distinction between Dhamma and non-Dhamma.
He who imputes an offense where there is no offense burns himself;
such an accuser knows neither discipline nor non-discipline.
One who is unskilled in discipline and non-discipline,
who imputes an offense where there is no offense—
such a reprover consumes himself.
One who does not know what has been said and what has not been said,
being unskilled in what has been said and what has not been said,
imputes an offense where there is no offense.
Such a reprover burns himself up;
he does not know what is practiced and what is not practiced,
being unskilled in what is practiced and what is not practiced.
One who imputes an offense where there is no offense burns himself; such an accuser destroys his own self.
He does not know what has been prescribed and what has not been prescribed.
One who is unskilled in what has been prescribed and what has not been prescribed,
and who imputes an offense where there is no offense—
such an accuser consumes himself.
He does not know what is an offense and what is not an offense;
he is unskilled in offenses and non-offenses. He imputes an offense where there is no offense.
Such a reprover burns himself;
he does not know what is light or grave,
being unskilled in what is light and what is grave.
One who charges another with an offense when there is no offense causes such an accuser to burn himself;
he does not distinguish between what is with remainder and what is without remainder.
One who is unskilled regarding what is with remainder and what is without remainder,
and who imputes an offense where there is no offense—
such a reprover consumes himself.
He does not know what is grave or what is minor;
he is unskilled in distinguishing between the grave and the minor;
he imputes an offense where there is no offense.
Such a reprover burns himself;
he does not understand what precedes and what follows, being unskilled in the sequence of what comes before and after.
One who imputes an offense where there is no offense burns himself;
such an accuser does not understand the sequence of the discourse.
One who is unskilled in the path of the underlying intent,
and who imputes an offense where there is no offense—
such an accuser consumes himself.
The Section on Formal Accusation is concluded.
Its summary verse is:
Formal accusation and investigation, and...
The Uposatha [chapter] begins with the root;
in the Codanaka-khaṇḍa,
they establish the Dispensation.
